title: Thermoregulation, hypoglycaemia and NEWTT2
blurb: Keep a newborn warm, protect at-risk babies from hypoglycaemia and use NEWTT2, red flags and parents' concerns to escalate a baby who is becoming unwell.
question: Zara, 4 hours old, was born at 37 weeks to a mother who took labetalol for hypertension. She is sleepy and her blood glucose is 1.6 mmol/L. Her NEWTT2 score is 2. What should the midwife do?

teach.body: A newborn has little fat and glycogen, a large surface area and an immature immune system, so cold, low blood glucose and infection can develop fast and with subtle signs: a baby who stops feeding or becomes less responsive. Formally, NEWTT2 is the British Association of Perinatal Medicine framework for a newborn early warning trigger and track (November 2023 update). In plain English: a chart that scores a baby's observations so that a worrying trend triggers a timed review. Parents' concerns are an important indicator of serious illness (NG194 1.4.1).

teach.caption: Keep newborns at 36.5-37.5 °C (RCUK 2025). Under 36 °C or 38 °C and over are red flags for serious illness (NG194 1.4.9).

teach.h: Thermal care at and after birth
items: 32 weeks or more: dry immediately, remove wet towels, put on a hat (RCUK 2025).
Under 32 weeks: dry the head and put on a hat, then place the body in a plastic bag without drying it.
Skin-to-skin as soon as possible after birth, keeping the baby warm and dry (NG235 1.11.7, 1.11.8).
Delivery room 23-25 °C for babies over 28 weeks; above 25 °C for 28 weeks or less.
A cold baby uses glucose and oxygen to make heat, so hypothermia and hypoglycaemia travel together.

teach.caption: At-risk babies: first glucose before the second feed (2-4 hours after birth), feeds no more than 3 hours apart, stay in hospital at least 24 hours.

head: Finding
Action
rows: Single value under 2.5 with abnormal signs
40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg plus a feed
More than two values under 2.0, no signs
teach.caption: NG3 (mother with diabetes): feed within 30 minutes of birth, then every 2-3 hours until pre-feed glucose is at least 2.0 mmol/L; test at 2-4 hours; not discharged before 24 hours and feeding well.

steps.label: Score 6+ or any critical
steps.sub: Immediate review; any critical obs: consider 2222

teach.caption: Healthcare professional concern can trigger a review at any score, and parental concern is scored on the chart. A blood glucose of 2.6 mmol/L or more scores 0.

teach.h: Red flags: illness and early-onset infection

rows.label: Other
values: Infection in a twin or triplet sibling

teach.caption: NG195: any red flag, or two or more non-red-flag factors, means antibiotics without waiting for results, given within 1 hour of the decision (benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin first line).

teach.h: Worked scenario: Zara on the postnatal ward
teach.body: Zara is at risk because her mother took labetalol, a beta-blocker. The first question is whether her sleepiness is an abnormal clinical sign: if she is hard to rouse or will not feed, a value under 2.5 mmol/L with abnormal signs needs urgent neonatal review and treatment. If she rouses and feeds normally, 1.6 mmol/L falls in the 1.0-1.9 band, so the midwife gives 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg, supports a feed straight away and rechecks glucose per protocol. A NEWTT2 score of 2 also needs a Tier 1 review within 1 hour, and the midwife records the score, the plan and the time to recheck.

teach.text: Do not be falsely reassured by a low total score. NEWTT2 lets healthcare professional concern trigger a review at any score, parental concern is scored on the chart, and any single critical observation needs immediate review. And do not mix up the numbers: 2.0 mmol/L is the operational threshold for pre-feed glucose, but a value under 2.5 with abnormal signs is treated, and under 1.0 is an emergency.

items: Normal newborn temperature 36.5-37.5 °C; under 36 or 38 °C and over is a red flag.
At risk of hypoglycaemia: preterm, growth restricted, maternal diabetes, maternal beta-blockers.
First glucose before the second feed (2-4 h); feeds no more than 3 hours apart.
1.0-1.9 without signs: 40% gel 200 mg/kg plus feed; under 1.0 or under 2.5 with signs: urgent treatment.
NEWTT2: 1 repeat in 1 h; 2-3 review in 1 h; 4-5 within 15 min; 6+ immediate. Concern can override.

summary: You can now keep a newborn within the normal temperature range, identify babies at risk of hypoglycaemia and act on their glucose results. You can also use NEWTT2 scores, red flags and parents' concerns to escalate a baby at the right speed.

A.q: A midwife is explaining thermal care to a student. Within which temperature range should a newborn baby be kept?
A.why: RCUK 2025 newborn guidance: keep the newborn's temperature between 36.5 and 37.5 °C.

whyNot.0: 36.0 °C is too low; the lower limit of normal is 36.5 °C.
whyNot.1: This range is hypothermic; under 36 °C is a red flag (NG194 1.4.9).
whyNot.2: 37.5 °C is the upper limit, and 38 °C or over is a red flag.

A.q: Hana has type 1 diabetes and has just given birth at term to a well baby. What feeding plan does NICE NG3 recommend?
options: Feed within 2 hours of birth, then every 4 hours
Feed within 30 minutes, then every 2–3 hours
Feed on demand, with a glucose check at 12 hours
Formula top-up after each breastfeed from birth
A.why: NG3 1.5.9: babies of women with diabetes should feed as soon as possible after birth (within 30 minutes) and then at frequent intervals (every 2-3 hours) until pre-feed glucose is at least 2.0 mmol/L.

whyNot.0: Two hours to the first feed and 4-hourly feeds are too long for an at-risk baby.
whyNot.2: Glucose is tested at 2-4 hours after birth, not 12, and feeds are not left to demand alone.
whyNot.3: Routine formula top-ups are not the NG3 plan; early, frequent feeding is.

A.q: A baby on the postnatal ward has a NEWTT2 total score of 4. What response is required?
options: Repeat the observations within 1 hour
Tier 1 review within 1 hour
Review within 15 minutes
Recheck at the next routine feed
A.why: NEWTT2 (Nov 2023): a score of 4-5 needs review within 15 minutes.

whyNot.0: Repeating observations within 1 hour is the response to a score of 1.
whyNot.1: A Tier 1 review within 1 hour is the response to a score of 2-3.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a routine feed delays a required 15-minute review.

B.q: Ivy, 3 hours old, is at risk of hypoglycaemia because her mother took labetalol. She is alert, with no abnormal signs, and her glucose is 1.6 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give 40% glucose gel and support a feed
Recheck the glucose after the next full feed
Arrange transfer for IV dextrose now
Give formula and stop glucose checks
B.why: BAPM framework: for a glucose of 1.0-1.9 mmol/L without abnormal signs, give 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg and a feed, then recheck.

whyNot.1: A value of 1.6 mmol/L needs treatment now, not just a later recheck.
whyNot.2: IV dextrose is for values under 1.0 mmol/L or abnormal signs; gel plus feed is first line here.
whyNot.3: Stopping monitoring in an at-risk baby with a low value is unsafe.

B.q: A baby at risk of hypoglycaemia has a blood glucose of 0.9 mmol/L at 3 hours. What should the midwife do?
options: Give glucose gel and recheck in 1 hour
Support a breastfeed and recheck pre-feed
Call for urgent neonatal team review
Repeat the test to confirm the value
B.why: BAPM: a glucose under 1.0 mmol/L at any time needs urgent treatment, so the neonatal team must review the baby urgently.

whyNot.0: Gel plus feed is the plan for 1.0-1.9 mmol/L without abnormal signs, not under 1.0.
whyNot.1: Feeding support alone does not treat a value under 1.0 mmol/L.
whyNot.3: Repeating the test delays urgent treatment of a dangerously low value.

B.q: Theo, 6 hours old, has an axillary temperature of 35.8 °C and is feeding poorly. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Add a hat and recheck in 4 hours
Urgent review, as under 36 °C is a red flag
Record it, as this is a normal newborn value
Bath him in warm water to rewarm him
B.why: NG194 1.4.9 lists a temperature under 36 °C as a red flag for serious illness in a young baby, and poor feeding is a change in behaviour (1.4.7), so he needs urgent review.

whyNot.0: Warming measures help, but a red-flag temperature needs urgent review, not a 4-hour wait.
whyNot.2: 35.8 °C is below the normal range of 36.5-37.5 °C.
whyNot.3: Bathing a cold baby increases heat loss; skin-to-skin and review are needed.

C.q: Baby Omar, 20 hours old, has a NEWTT2 score of 1. His parents say he is 'not himself' and has been floppy since the last feed. What should the midwife do?
options: Repeat observations within 1 hour as for a score of 1
Ask for a medical review now despite the low score
Explain that a low score means he is well
Re-score after the next feed in 3 hours
C.why: NEWTT2 lets healthcare professional concern trigger a review at any score; NICE NG194 1.4.1 says to treat parents' concerns as an important indicator of possible serious illness, and floppiness is a change in the baby's signs (1.4.7).

whyNot.0: The score-1 response ignores the parents' concern and a change in tone that warrant review now.
whyNot.2: A low score does not override concern about floppiness and altered behaviour.
whyNot.3: Waiting 3 hours delays review of a possible serious illness.

C.q: Lila was born after prolonged rupture of membranes. At 8 hours old she has an episode of apnoea. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start antibiotics within 1 hour of the decision
Observe for 12 hours before deciding
Wait for blood culture results before treating
Use the Kaiser calculator to decide on antibiotics
C.why: Apnoea is an NG195 red flag; any red flag means starting antibiotics without waiting for results, within 1 hour of the decision (NG195 1.10.3, 1.15.2).

whyNot.1: 12 hours of observation is for one risk factor without a red flag.
whyNot.2: Antibiotics must not wait for culture results when a red flag is present.
whyNot.3: NG195 limits the Kaiser calculator to babies over 34 weeks within prospective audit; a red flag means treat.

C.q: Ezra, 5 hours old, is growth restricted. He is lethargic and not rousing for feeds. His blood glucose is 2.3 mmol/L. How should this result be interpreted?
options: Reassuring, as it is above 2.0
Hypoglycaemia needing treatment now
Recheck it before the next 3-hourly feed
Give gel if the next result is under 2.0
C.why: BAPM: a single value under 2.5 mmol/L with abnormal clinical signs is treated as hypoglycaemia; lethargy and not rousing for feeds are abnormal signs.

whyNot.0: 2.0 mmol/L is the threshold for well babies; with abnormal signs the trigger is under 2.5.
whyNot.2: Waiting for the next feed delays treatment of symptomatic hypoglycaemia.
whyNot.3: Treatment is needed now because he has abnormal signs with a value under 2.5.

reteach.title: Warm, fed, watched
reteach.question: Think of three jobs for every newborn in the first day. What are they, and what tells you one is failing?

blocks.body: Warm: keep 36.5-37.5 °C with skin-to-skin, hats and dry towels. Fed: at-risk babies feed early and at least 3-hourly, with glucose checked before the second feed. Watched: NEWTT2 observations, red flags and what the parents notice. A baby who is cold, will not feed or is less responsive is telling you one job is failing, and the response is timed escalation, not waiting.

blocks.text: Concern beats the number: a parent saying 'he is not himself' is recorded as parental concern on the NEWTT2 chart, and your own professional concern can trigger a review even when the total is 0 or 1.

explain.body: Aim for 36.5-37.5 °C. At 32 weeks or more, dry, remove wet towels, add a hat, then skin-to-skin. Under 32 weeks, dry the head and add a hat but put the body in a plastic bag without drying it (RCUK 2025).

test.q: A baby is born at 30 weeks. Which thermal care step is correct?
options: Dry the body well, then wrap in two warm towels
Bath promptly to remove the vernix
Place the body in a plastic bag without drying
Lay the baby naked under a fan heater
test.why: RCUK 2025: under 32 weeks, dry the head and put on a hat, then place the body in a plastic bag without drying.

whyNot.0: Drying and wrapping is the approach for babies of 32 weeks or more.
whyNot.1: Bathing causes heat loss and is not part of immediate care.
whyNot.3: Fan heaters move air and increase heat loss; a plastic bag reduces it.

explain.h: Who is at risk of low glucose
explain.body: BAPM at-risk groups: preterm, growth restricted, mothers with diabetes, mothers taking beta-blockers such as labetalol. Check glucose before the second feed, feed no more than 3 hours apart, and keep them in hospital for at least 24 hours.

test.q: Which baby is in a BAPM risk group for neonatal hypoglycaemia?
options: Born at 40 weeks with a weight of 3.4 kg
Mother took labetalol in pregnancy
Mother had an epidural in labour
Born by planned caesarean at term
test.why: Maternal beta-blockers such as labetalol are a BAPM risk factor, alongside prematurity, growth restriction and maternal diabetes.

whyNot.0: A term baby of normal weight has no listed risk factor.
whyNot.2: An epidural is not a listed hypoglycaemia risk factor.
whyNot.3: Planned caesarean birth is not a listed hypoglycaemia risk factor.

explain.body: Score 1: repeat observations within 1 hour. 2-3: Tier 1 review within 1 hour. 4-5: review within 15 minutes. 6 or more: immediate review. Any critical (purple) observation: immediate review and consider a 2222 call. Healthcare professional concern can trigger a review at any score.

test.q: A baby's NEWTT2 total is 6. What response is required?
options: Review within 15 minutes
Tier 1 review within the next hour
Repeat observations in 1 hour
Request an immediate review
test.why: NEWTT2 (Nov 2023) escalation table: a score of 6 or more needs an immediate review by the Tier 1 doctor or ANNP, with the Tier 2 informed; a 2222 call is considered for any critical (purple) observation.

whyNot.0: Review within 15 minutes is for a score of 4-5.
whyNot.1: A Tier 1 review within 1 hour is for a score of 2-3.
whyNot.2: Repeating observations in 1 hour is for a score of 1.

explain.body: NG194 1.4.9 red flags include appearing ill, pale or mottled skin, being unrousable, a weak or high-pitched cry, grunting, respiratory rate over 60, chest indrawing, temperature under 36 or 38 °C and over, a bulging fontanelle and seizures. Any red flag needs urgent medical assessment.

test.q: Which finding in a 2-day-old baby is an NG194 red flag for serious illness?
options: Temperature of 37.2 °C
Respiratory rate of 66 per minute
Feeding 9 times in 24 hours
Sleeping for 2–3 hours between feeds
test.why: NG194 1.4.9 lists an increased respiratory rate over 60 breaths per minute as a red flag.

whyNot.0: 37.2 °C is within the normal range of 36.5-37.5 °C.
whyNot.2: Frequent feeding (8-12 times a day) is expected in the early weeks.
whyNot.3: Sleeping between feeds is normal newborn behaviour.
